title: Bear Day Afternoon #broadway #dogdayafternoon #thebear #theatre
transcript: So how does the Broadway version of Dog Day Afternoon, starring John Bernthal and Ebon Moss-Bachrach from The Bear compare to the original Al Pacino film? On paper, everything about this seemed to be a layup: The cast is great, the material lends itself well to being staged as a play, and it seemed right in the wheelhouse of Pulitzer winning playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis, who adapted the script. I’ve had a weird journey with this play over the last couple days because I mostly enjoyed the experience of watching it, but I was vaguely aware that word of mouth  from the theatre community was kind of negative. So the very next day I rewatched the film for the first time in like five years, and unfortunately the side by side comparison forced me to acknowledge that a lot of the criticisms were spot on. I remember there being something of a comedic undertone to the film as Sonny is kind of inept, kind of well-meaning, and ultimately kind of endearing to the bank employees even as he's holding them hostage. And maybe that's why it didn't initially ping to me as weird that the play had a lot more comedy in it. But in retrospect, yes, the humor in the stage play is a lot more emphasized and not very successful. I think I would mostly attribute that to Rupert Goold’s direction, but I also didn't realize in the moment just how much Guirgis wrote for this adaptation. Maybe the most holistic difference, aside from the humor, is that the film stays pretty focused on Sonny, whereas Guirgis makes it more of an ensemble piece and adds a lot of material for the supporting characters, which actually makes a lot of sense for the medium of stage plays. And a lot of that added material worked fine for me on its own terms. But there's a “less is more” quality to the original that gets muddied up and overburdened here by Guirgis’s adaptation. But then the question is, why did I enjoy the play while watching it? Well, I would still probably maintain that the core of this story is quite compelling. I might be a bit biased because there's a specific narrative device/trope/dynamic whatever you wanna call it, that I have a particular fondness for. It’s the thing where people who are in opposition to each other still have a mutual respect and don't wanna cause harm. And we see some of that here with the cop, played by John Ortiz, who is using the sort of nice guy routine with Sonny. But more so it's the relationship between Sonny and the hostages where he's, like, determined to make them feel safe, even though that's kind of against the whole point. And not only does that make him a more interesting character, but it adds tension to the situation that you wouldn't have otherwise. And I think both Guirgis’ adaptation and John Bernthal's powerhouse performance do a reasonably good job carrying over that dynamic from the original story. Speaking of performances, a lot of people are saying that Ebon Moss-Bachrach is kind of underutilized in the mostly quiet role of Sal, Sonny’s accomplice, especially when it might have been more intuitive to cast him as the cop. But I can also appreciate that there's a different kind of power in a character like Sal. His looming presence has this chilling effect on the room. And when he does speak, there's weight behind his words. In many ways, it's a more challenging role for the actor without really feeding their ego as much, so I respect it. One thing I was questioning even while watching the play is that while the material definitely works as a stage play, it lends itself well to it. I wasn't sure if there was much gained by it, but the moment that partly changed my mind on that is when they kind of cast us, the audience, in the role of the spectators outside the bank. And Guirgis writes an admittedly heavy-handed but still impactful speech that really hammers home this point about the relationship between law enforcement and the public eye. Interestingly, though, in the film, Sonny has Even more interactions with the crowd than he does in the play, which seems like maybe a missed opportunity.
reasoning: The reviewer has a conflicted experience - enjoyed watching it but acknowledges the criticisms are valid after comparing to the film. He finds positives in the performances and core story but notes significant flaws in the adaptation's humor and structure.
